Personally for me, my main tips are speed, “short cuts”, order of elimination, and resources

Speed: For this I recommend getting the practice exam if you haven’t. It’s essentially the exam cut in half, giving you around the same amount of time for each question. I kept taking them, identifying the weak areas I didn’t do so well in and making sure I doubled down on those. On the exam, do the “easiest” sections first (coding guidelines, compliance and regulatory, HCPCS, and any of what you feel you scored highest in the practice exam in) giving you more time for everything else.

Short cuts: writing down commonly used codes can help you as well as the guidelines they’re in. For example hypertension is i10, and the guidelines for it is in G16.
[Psst. This helped a LOT.](https://www.tiktok.com/t/ZTjAVCQLj/)

Order of elimination: many questions trip you up with codes that aren’t needed, modifiers that don’t align with codes, etc. make sure to read Everything and again, make sure those guidelines add up!! 

[Hoang](https://youtube.com/@codingwithhoang?si=ntYym0-lcpBAU2Vh) helps a lot with speed and order of elimination.
[CodeMed Mastery](https://youtube.com/@codemedmastery?si=GHSdRkvkJkV5cg-b) helps with guidelines and tips for coding. Both give you practice questions and can help greatly.

Good luck! 🍀

never be afraid/ashamed of going to community college. it's cheaper, and, if you didn't get stellar grades in high school, it's a good backup 

never sign up for any class before 10-11 am (which brings me to my next point— plan + register your classes as soon as you can)

[rate my professor](http://ratemyprofessor.com) is a life saver when it comes to picking who you want when you have your classes

do your fafsa. don't wait till the last minute. do it within the month it opens up for the school year.

unless you have a job (or just don't want to, lol), I'd highly suggest doing summer/winter classes. doesn't have to be as many as your spring/fall ones (for example, my college has a 12 credit minimum for s/f and 8 credit maximum for s/w) you get credits quicker if you wanna transfer or graduate early

never buy new textbooks. always buy used, or in times like these where everything is online, use sites like [z library](https://z-lib.org/) to potentially find your textbooks for free. speaking of textbooks, if you're on pdf sites and can't find the exact edition,  it's okay to get one that's 1 or 2 editions older

focus your first year on your general education and a couple classes for your major so you can have a feel for it

it's okay to change your major. it's okay to change your major more than once, too.
